Trump White House Warns Democrats Against Political Investigations: ‘Will Not Be Extorted or Cowed’
The White House issued a warning to congressional Democrats on Wednesday, declaring that President Trump’s administration will not tolerate politically motivated investigations or attempts to intimidate federal officials when Democrats take control of Congress in January.
White House Counsel Will Scharf delivered the message in a letter to Rep. Robert Garcia of California, who is expected to become chairman of the House Oversight Committee. The letter challenged Democrats’ plans to launch extensive investigations into the administration following their midterm election victories.
Scharf warned that congressional investigations must serve legitimate legislative purposes rather than function as tools for political retaliation or criminal prosecution. He argued that lawmakers could exceed their constitutional authority if they used subpoenas to harass government officials.
“The administration will not be extorted and will not be cowed,” Scharf wrote, making clear that the White House intends to challenge investigative actions it considers unlawful.
The warning followed Garcia’s public message to Trump administration officials after Democrats won control of Congress in the November 3 elections. The California Democrat told officials to “lawyer up,” signaling that congressional investigations and subpoenas would become a major priority under the incoming majority.
Other Democratic lawmakers have made similar statements. Rep. Analilia Mejia of New Jersey declared that Democrats would distribute subpoenas “like Mardi Gras beads,” while Illinois Rep. Delia Ramirez warned administration officials to clear their schedules.
Scharf cited those remarks as evidence of what the White House considers an effort to intimidate federal employees rather than conduct legitimate congressional oversight.
The White House counsel also warned that threats intended to interfere with the lawful functioning of government could potentially cross into criminal misconduct. He suggested that deliberately unlawful subpoenas could warrant further investigation.
Democrats are preparing to examine several areas of the Trump administration, including immigration enforcement, military operations involving Iran, and decisions made by senior White House officials.
Potential witnesses include former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, current DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, border czar Tom Homan, and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller.
Garcia rejected the White House’s warning, maintaining that Congress has broad constitutional authority to investigate the executive branch. He insisted that Democrats would proceed with their oversight plans despite the administration’s objections.
President Trump has already accused Democrats of threatening administration officials with impeachment and other forms of punishment without sufficient justification.
In a Truth Social post over the weekend, Trump described the planned investigations as extortion and called for accountability if lawmakers engaged in unlawful conduct.
Attorney General Todd Blanche has also addressed the controversy, acknowledging that Congress possesses legitimate oversight authority while warning that threatening behavior could raise separate legal concerns.
The dispute comes as Democrats prepare to assume control of both chambers of Congress following the Republican Party’s midterm losses. Their new majorities will give them greater authority to schedule hearings, issue subpoenas, and investigate executive branch decisions.
Congressional oversight is a recognized legislative function, but the Constitution also places limits on investigative authority. The Supreme Court has previously ruled that congressional subpoenas must serve legitimate legislative purposes, particularly when seeking information involving the president.
The White House’s letter does not establish that Democrats have violated those limits, and no criminal charges have been announced in connection with the planned investigations.
The confrontation signals an increasingly contentious relationship between President Trump and the incoming Democratic majority. With congressional control changing hands in January, the administration is preparing to defend its officials and policies against a potentially extensive series of investigations.
For now, the White House has made its position clear: it intends to resist congressional actions it considers politically motivated or unconstitutional while maintaining that legitimate oversight must remain within established legal boundaries.

Washington DC [US], November 12 (ANI): Incoming chairman of the US House Oversight Committee, Democratic Representative Robert Garcia, on Wednesday (local time), pushed back against the White House's warning of potential legal action over forthcoming congressional investigations into President Donald Trump and his allies, vowing an aggressive oversight approach when Democrats take control of the powerful committee in January.
Reacting to the warning in an interview with CNN, Garcia dismissed the administration's position, saying Democrats would not be intimidated from investigating the Trump administration and those associated with the President.
"Give me a break. I mean, they cannot take any sort of heat at this moment," Garcia told CNN, adding that the American public wanted Democrats to challenge the administration.
"What the American public wants is they want us to fight, and they want us to be in this moment where we are pushing back against someone who has tried to essentially install an authoritarian system," he said.
Garcia's remarks came after the White House sent a letter cautioning the incoming committee chairman against using congressional investigative powers beyond constitutional limits. According to CNN, which obtained a copy of the letter dated Monday, the administration warned that it "will not be extorted" through what it described as unlawful congressional processes.
However, a source familiar with the matter told CNN that Garcia had not received the letter from the White House.
The letter, signed by White House Counsel Will Scharf, stated that the administration expected lawmakers to conduct investigations within established constitutional boundaries.
"The Trump Administration expects members of Congress to discharge their investigative functions within settled constitutional limits," the letter stated, as quoted by CNN.
It further warned: "The Administration will not be extorted and will not be cowed by unlawful process motivated by animus, pettiness, hatred, or any other unlawful motive to intimidate, penalise or interfere with the lawful functioning of government."
Scharf also argued that threatening executive branch officials to discourage them from public service could amount to "blatant criminality". The letter maintained that congressional investigations must serve legitimate legislative purposes and cannot be used to exercise criminal prosecution powers assigned to the Executive and the Judiciary.
Garcia, however, defended the need for congressional scrutiny and said those who had allegedly harmed the American public should be prepared to face investigations.
"If you have abused the American public, you should lawyer up. If you’re a corporate CEO and you’re ripping off the American people, you should lawyer up. The incoming Democratic committee leaders have indicated that their investigations could cover a broad range of issues, including members of Trump's Cabinet and his family.

Raskin said Democrats remained committed to exercising congressional oversight powers, declaring that they were "obviously undeterred and unbowed and uncowed."

"We have to know what’s going on in the government. We need to know what’s going on in the economy, what’s going on in the society in order to pass the laws that the American people need," he said, as quoted by CNN.

White House Letter Puts Criminality Claim at Center of Coming House Oversight Fight - FINCHANNEL
sources.text:
The FINANCIAL — the White House oversight warning to the Democrat expected to lead the House’s principal investigative committee has set the terms for an early confrontation between the Trump administration and a new congressional majority, with the president’s chief lawyer saying some planned inquiries could cross into criminal conduct.
Will Scharf, the White House counsel, sent a letter dated Nov. 9 to Representative Robert Garcia of California, the senior Democrat on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform. The letter said that congressional investigation must serve a legitimate legislative purpose and warned that threats directed at executive-branch officials or subpoenas used to deny constitutional rights could warrant further investigation, according to CBS News.
The letter arrived after Democrats won control of the House in last week’s midterm elections and as Garcia is expected to become chairman when the new Congress convenes in January. It is an unusually direct pre-emptive warning from the executive branch before the committee has opened any new investigation or issued a subpoena.
Garcia rejected the premise in a statement, saying that Congress’s investigative authority flows from Article I of the Constitution and does not require White House permission. He said Democrats would not be deterred from examining alleged corruption and abuse. The exchange makes clear that the conflict will concern the scope and purpose of congressional oversight as much as any particular investigation.
Scharf’s letter did not announce a criminal case or name any lawmaker as a target. It referred instead to potential conduct that, in the administration’s view, could exceed constitutional boundaries. The warning was directed at anticipated oversight, not an existing House demand.
The White House had previewed the administration’s argument days earlier in a Nov. 8 release about Attorney General Todd Blanche’s television appearances. Blanche said the Justice Department would represent executive-branch officials called before Congress and argued that Democrats had threatened investigations, impeachments and private citizens. The release framed the disagreement as one over oversight and political retaliation.
Blanche also said that the Justice Department has represented executive-branch officials in congressional proceedings in every administration. That statement describes a familiar institutional role: the department provides legal representation to federal officials in matters connected to their official duties. The newer issue is the White House’s contention that an investigation or subpoena could itself create grounds for an inquiry.
Congress has broad powers to obtain information relevant to legislation, appropriations and oversight. But those powers are not unlimited. The Supreme Court has said that Congress’s power to investigate is inherent in the legislative process, while also holding that an inquiry must be related to and in furtherance of a legitimate legislative task.
The court’s 2020 decision in Trump v. Mazars USA addressed congressional subpoenas for a president’s personal information. The justices did not erase Congress’s investigative authority. Instead, they required courts to weigh separation-of-powers concerns when a congressional subpoena seeks a president’s personal records, including whether the legislative purpose justifies the information sought and whether the request is no broader than reasonably necessary.
That decision is likely to be part of the legal background to any dispute involving documents or testimony from the White House. It does not, however, provide a simple rule for every future committee inquiry. Each subpoena and claim of privilege can turn on the records requested, the committee’s stated purpose and the constitutional interests at stake.
Scharf’s letter cited public comments by Democrats about their plans for oversight. CBS reported that he said these statements showed an intent to use investigative processes to harass or aggrandize rather than advance a legitimate legislative end. The White House counsel wrote that processes designed to abuse or instill fear could cross the line into “blatant criminality.”
Democrats have discussed possible examinations of administration actions involving immigration enforcement, the conflict with Iran, the Epstein investigation, White House construction, mineral policy and cryptocurrency-related matters. None of those prospective inquiries has yet been defined in a committee subpoena or hearing notice. Their eventual legal footing will depend on the particular authority asserted and the information requested.
The committee Garcia is in line to lead has expansive jurisdiction. The House’s official rules assign it responsibility for oversight and investigations across federal government activities, as well as issues involving government management, procurement and ethics. Its authority gives its chairman a platform to seek documents and call officials, but committee actions are also governed by House rules and are subject to legal challenges.
Republicans retain their own institutional role on the committee. James Comer of Kentucky, the current chairman, said in reporting on the White House letter that the panel must remain an independent check on the executive branch, while criticizing Garcia’s rhetoric. The comment illustrated that the dispute is not limited to the White House and Democrats; it also involves how the committee itself will operate after control changes hands.
For the administration, the immediate objective appears to be to establish a legal and political record before the next Congress begins. The letter asserts that the executive branch will scrutinize whether investigative demands have a legislative purpose. It also signals that the White House expects officials and private parties to resist requests it considers improper.
For Democrats, the letter offers an early preview of the obstacles they may face in translating campaign promises into oversight. Committee leaders can request information, conduct hearings and issue subpoenas under House procedures. But executive agencies can object, withhold materials on privilege grounds, negotiate limits or challenge demands in court.

Democrats' Investigations Could Constitute 'Blatant Criminality,' Says White House Counsel
Democrats have warned the administration to "lawyer up" and prepare for "subpoenas." The White House countered that this could be illegal.
After last week's midterm elections swept them into power across the country, Democrats pledged to conduct aggressive oversight of President Donald Trump and members of his administration.
This week, a White House official suggested that conducting investigations, or even threatening to do so, could be illegal.
On election night, as the returns indicated sizable Democratic gains in both the House and Senate, Rep. Robert Garcia (D–Calif.), the ranking member on the House Oversight Committee and its likely next chairman, wrote a simple message on X: "LAWYER UP." Added Sen. Ron Wyden (D–Ore.), likely the next chairman of the Senate Finance Committee: "Subpoenas."
In the week after the midterms, numerous top officials at the Department of Justice (DOJ) resigned, though the department insists its work will continue.
Unsurprisingly, this did not sit well with the president. Over the weekend, he wrote on Truth Social that this was "extortion at the highest level" for which Democrats should face "imprisonment," and he called for the DOJ to investigate. Attorney General Todd Blanche agreed, though as Reason's Jacob Sullum notes, neither Trump nor Blanche could articulate how routine political rhetoric rose to the level of any crime, extortion or otherwise.
Then this week, the White House warned that even calls for investigating Republicans could be against the law.
"I write to remind you of the foundational limits that the Constitution imposes on congressional investigations and subpoenas, which you and members of the new Congress have evinced a clear intent to transgress," White House counsel William Scharf wrote in a letter to Garcia that was first reported by Punchbowl News. "We are monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators who seek to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government."
Kyle Cheney and Chris Marquette at Politico called the letter "a departure from precedent, as the Justice Department is typically the front line for engaging with Congress on matters related to congressional oversight."
Scharf cited a number of instances, like Garcia's "lawyer up" post, when Democratic lawmakers have pledged to go after the administration.
"We're going to be passing out subpoenas like candy," Rep. Emily Randall (D–Wash.), for example, wrote on BlueSky. Sen. Ed Markey (D–Mass.) added, "They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we'll be printing."
Of course, these are the kinds of things that politicians say about their opponents all the time. Heated political rhetoric can be obnoxious, but it is generally a protected form of speech.
This, says Scharf, is different. "Abusive threats and public statements about the indiscriminate issuance of subpoenas, along with threats directed at prospective targets within the Administration make it abundantly clear that any forthcoming investigative processes will be deployed to harass and aggrandize, rather than to advance any legitimate legislative end," the letter warned. "Threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality. And issuing unlawful subpoenas with the intention of depriving citizens of their constitutional rights and privileges may warrant further investigation."
Writing on social media, New York University law professor Ryan Goodman called the letter "legally repulsive." He added that it ignores the Speech or Debate Clause from Article I, Section 6 of the U.S. Constitution, which legally protects members of Congress "for any Speech or Debate in either House." The U.S. Supreme Court has broadly applied the rule to anything that lawmakers say in the course of their legislative duties.
Princeton University law professor Deborah Pearlstein agreed, calling Scharf's letter a "particularly ham-fisted stab at intimidation" that was "worth the paper it's written on, not more."
It's also particularly rich for the Trump administration to suggest that threatening a political opponent with investigation or impeachment is, itself, grounds for reprisal. After all, Trump routinely does just that, and worse.
Put aside for a moment the irony that Trump's response to being threatened with investigation is to, in turn, threaten investigations right back. In his second term, the government indicted former FBI Director James Comey, a longtime Trump foe, three separate times, in increasingly desperate fashion.
In a Truth Social post last year that was reportedly intended as a private message to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi, Trump raged that "nothing is being done" about people like Comey, Sen. Adam Schiff (D–Calif.), and New York Attorney General Letitia James.
Last year, six Democratic lawmakers with military service, including Sens. Elissa Slotkin (D–Mich.) and Mark Kelly (D–Ariz.), recorded a video reminding those in active duty, "You can refuse illegal orders."
While that message should have been completely anodyne, the president took offense. "It's called SEDITIOUS BEHAVIOR AT THE HIGHEST LEVEL. Each one of these traitors to our Country should be ARRESTED AND PUT ON TRIAL," he wrote in one post, adding in another, "SEDITIOUS BEHAVIOR, punishable by DEATH!"
It's also quite ironic for Trump to say that Democrats "going around threatening a lot of people…with Impeachment" constitutes "extortion at the highest level." While campaigning in 2024, the then-former president said "Congress ought to impeach crooked Joe Biden," and that once reelected he would "appoint a real special 'prosecutor'" to go after Biden.
He also admitted that the calls to impeach Biden were directly related to his own two impeachments during his first term. At that time, he had said lawmakers like Schiff and Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D–Calif.) had committed "High Crimes and Misdemeanors, and even Treason" and "must all be immediately Impeached!" (Members of Congress can be censured or removed but not impeached.)
This is not to say that Democrats are completely justified in their efforts. As Reason's Tosin Akintola noted this week, Democrats plan to expand their investigations beyond federal officials to include private companies that have done business with the administration, including perhaps under duress.
But to suggest that any pledge to investigate the administration could constitute extortion or any other crime is laughable, an affront to the constitutional principles of both free speech and the separation of powers.
"Let's be clear: Congress' authority comes from Article I of the Constitution, not from the permission of the White House. Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate," Garcia told Politico in a statement. "We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President's lawyers."

The letter, obtained from a White House official, marks the latest escalation from the Trump administration ahead of Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress next year. It also dovetails with years of Trump’s threats to prosecute his critics.
“We are monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators who seek to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government,” the letter says.
Garcia, the likely committee chair next Congress, pushed back on the threat in a statement Wednesday, accusing the administration of having “something to hide” and that Congress has wide authority to investigate the executive branch.

The letter came after Attorney General Todd Blanche previously refused to rule out criminal charges against members of Congress in response to investigations.
“It depends on what the crime is and what they have done,” Blanche told CNN over the weekend.
Last week, President Donald Trump himself said that threats of investigations and impeachment were “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”
He also singled out Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., calling for her to be imprisoned. The administration previously unsuccessfully attempted to indict Slotkin and other Democrats over a video she published calling for soldiers to disobey illegal orders.

Schiff, D-Calif., to face unspecified charges in a post on Truth Social addressed to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi that also called for the prosecution of former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James. Both have faced criminal charges, pleaded not guilty and fought them in court as political attacks.

But House and Senate committees under both parties have broad authority to investigate a range of matters, and they’ve rarely been stopped by the courts.
Likely House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., called the Scharf letter “outrageous,” telling reporters on Capitol Hill on Wednesday: “It’s factually inaccurate. It’s legally inaccurate, and it’s inaccurate in terms of the Constitution.”
“A Democratic Congress is going to be a check and balance on an out-of-control executive branch in the face of unprecedented corruption that they’ve unleashed on the American people. And if they don’t like it, consult the Constitution,” Jeffries said.

Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., and other Democrats telling service members not to follow illegal orders amounted to “SEDITIOUS BEHAVIOR, punishable by DEATH!”

By Erin Banco and Jonathan Landay
WASHINGTON, Nov 10 (Reuters) – Democrats in the US House of Representatives, who will control key committees next year, are preparing investigations into what they say was President Donald Trump’s politicization and gutting of US spy agencies, including whether analysts have censored themselves to avoid retaliation.
“There’s absolutely evidence that analysts are hesitant to write on topics that they think might be controversial. There’s absolutely evidence of a decline in morale in the analytic community because of the pressures that they are under,” US Representative Jim Himes, a Connecticut Democrat who will become chairman of the House intelligence committee in January, told Reuters on Tuesday.
There has been little scrutiny of the state of the US intelligence community by the Republican-run Congress during the first two years of Trump’s second term, during which the administration fired or forced out hundreds of officers and disrupted the production of analyses on key issues, including Iran.
Himes said that would change after he takes over the committee in January, when Democrats assume control of the House of Representatives and the Senate following their sweep of the November 3 midterm elections.
He did not disclose how the investigations would proceed, but said that one focus would be what he called retaliatory firings.
“We’re going to tell the story of the patriots who were fired because they said something that was inconsistent with what the president wanted to be true,” Himes said.
Former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard last year cut her agency’s staff by about 40%. CIA Director John Ratcliffe publicly pledged to reduce his workforce by more than 1,000 positions over several years. Both offered deferred-resignation programs that provided pay and benefits for employees who chose to leave.
The cuts included the firings of longtime intelligence analysts and officers from top posts, including at the National Intelligence Council, the analytical group overseen by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.
At least two of those fired were analysts involved in an assessment that contradicted the White House’s official policy on Venezuela.
The reductions have been viewed inside the intelligence agencies as a continuation of Trump’s campaign against what he called the “deep state,” a move critics say has drained the community of experience and expertise.
Reuters previously reported that some of Gabbard’s projects affiliated with her Director’s Initiative Group, a task force that revisited the 2020 election and the origins of COVID-19, created tensions inside the intelligence community.
BREAKDOWN IN INTELLIGENCE SHARING
That was particularly the case after Gabbard’s office revoked the security clearances of current and former intelligence officials a year ago.
Gabbard’s actions caused a breakdown in intelligence sharing and cooperation inside the intelligence community and with Congress, as Reuters previously reported.
“The moment the intelligence community stops telling the truth to national leaders, you get into an Iraq war because of weapons of mass destruction that don’t exist,” Himes said.
Himes said he had reviewed a statutorily mandated intelligence community survey showing that, in 2025, the workforce had begun to “feel very real political pressure.”
He added he was working to declassify other internal intelligence community reporting that could potentially underscore the effects of the firings and politicization.
The committee, Himes said, will also probe the administration’s relationships with defense and intelligence contractors and US covert efforts overseas.
(Reporting by Erin Banco and Jonathan Landay; Editing by Don Durfee and Sanjeev Miglani)

The message from White House counsel Will Scharf to Rep. Robert Garcia, a California Democrat who is set to chair the Oversight Committee as of January, foreshadows a brewing fight between the Trump administration and congressional Democrats, who are poised to launch investigations in a slew of issues arising over the first two years of Mr. Trump's second term.
Scharf sent a letter to Garcia, dated Monday, reminding him that investigative acts by Congress must be backed by a "legitimate legislative purpose."
"Beyond being inconsistent with the clear, well-recognized constitutional limitations on your investigative functions, threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality," Scharf wrote. "And issuing unlawful subpoenas with the intention of depriving citizens of their constitutional rights and privileges may warrant further investigation."
Scharf cited recent statements from Democratic members of Congress who previewed investigations into the Trump administration they plan to pursue once they take control of the House and Senate. He claimed that Democrats are intent on crossing the Constitution's limits on congressional investigations and subpoenas.
"Abusive threats and public statements about the indiscriminate issuance of subpoenas, along with threats directed at prospective targets within the Administration make it abundantly clear that any forthcoming investigative processes will be deployed to harass and aggrandize rather than to advance any legitimate end," he wrote.
Scharf accused Democrats of making "abusive and capricious threats" and said they are seeking to "abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with lawful functioning of government."
Garcia said in response to Scharf that the White House is threatening to infringe on his committee's right to conduct oversight.

"Let's be clear: Congress' authority comes from Article I of the Constitution, not from the permission of the White House. Garcia accused the Trump administration of weaponizing the executive branch against Congress.

sources.news_title: House Democrats to investigate Trump’s handling of US spy agencies
sources.text:
By Erin Banco and Jonathan Landay
WASHINGTON, Nov 10 (Reuters) – Democrats in the US House of Representatives, who will control key committees next year, are preparing investigations into what they say was President Donald Trump’s politicization and gutting of US spy agencies, including whether analysts have censored themselves to avoid retaliation.
“There’s absolutely evidence that analysts are hesitant to write on topics that they think might be controversial. There’s absolutely evidence of a decline in morale in the analytic community because of the pressures that they are under,” US Representative Jim Himes, a Connecticut Democrat who will become chairman of the House intelligence committee in January, told Reuters on Tuesday.
There has been little scrutiny of the state of the US intelligence community by the Republican-run Congress during the first two years of Trump’s second term, during which the administration fired or forced out hundreds of officers and disrupted the production of analyses on key issues, including Iran.
Himes said that would change after he takes over the committee in January, when Democrats assume control of the House of Representatives and the Senate following their sweep of the November 3 midterm elections.
He did not disclose how the investigations would proceed, but said that one focus would be what he called retaliatory firings.
“We’re going to tell the story of the patriots who were fired because they said something that was inconsistent with what the president wanted to be true,” Himes said.
Former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard last year cut her agency’s staff by about 40%. CIA Director John Ratcliffe publicly pledged to reduce his workforce by more than 1,000 positions over several years. Both offered deferred-resignation programs that provided pay and benefits for employees who chose to leave.
The cuts included the firings of longtime intelligence analysts and officers from top posts, including at the National Intelligence Council, the analytical group overseen by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.
At least two of those fired were analysts involved in an assessment that contradicted the White House’s official policy on Venezuela.
The reductions have been viewed inside the intelligence agencies as a continuation of Trump’s campaign against what he called the “deep state,” a move critics say has drained the community of experience and expertise.
Reuters previously reported that some of Gabbard’s projects affiliated with her Director’s Initiative Group, a task force that revisited the 2020 election and the origins of COVID-19, created tensions inside the intelligence community.
BREAKDOWN IN INTELLIGENCE SHARING
That was particularly the case after Gabbard’s office revoked the security clearances of current and former intelligence officials a year ago.
Gabbard’s actions caused a breakdown in intelligence sharing and cooperation inside the intelligence community and with Congress, as Reuters previously reported.
“The moment the intelligence community stops telling the truth to national leaders, you get into an Iraq war because of weapons of mass destruction that don’t exist,” Himes said.
Himes said he had reviewed a statutorily mandated intelligence community survey showing that, in 2025, the workforce had begun to “feel very real political pressure.”
He added he was working to declassify other internal intelligence community reporting that could potentially underscore the effects of the firings and politicization.
The committee, Himes said, will also probe the administration’s relationships with defense and intelligence contractors and US covert efforts overseas.
(Reporting by Erin Banco and Jonathan Landay; Editing by Don Durfee and Sanjeev Miglani)

- The White House’s top lawyer said House Democrats could be criminally investigated if they launch investigations without a ‘legitimate legislative purpose.’

WASHINGTON — The White House’s top lawyer has warned House Democrats that their planned investigations into President Trump could expose them to criminal action, a threat that serves as an early sign of how combative the administration intends to be once Democrats take control of the House in January.
White House counsel Will Scharf raised the possibility of criminal inquiries into Democratic lawmakers in a letter Monday to Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Long Beach), who is expected to lead the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee next year.
Scharf argued that Democrats’ public promises to investigate and subpoena Trump administration officials “may cross the line into blatant criminality” and could amount to an illegal abuse of power if they do not identify “a legitimate” legislative purpose for their investigations.
He added that “issuing unlawful subpoenas with the intention of depriving citizens of their constitutional rights and privileges may warrant further investigation.”
While past administrations have resisted congressional subpoenas, Scharf’s letter goes further, suggesting that lawmakers who issue them could face criminal consequences — a claim legal experts say has little basis, given that the letter cites no specific crime and that the Constitution broadly protects congressional oversight.
President Trump and others in his administration have waffled in their public messaging on election integrity, immigration policy and other issues since the Republican Party’s massive losses in last week’s midterms.
Garcia dismissed the threats in the letter, calling it an attempt by the White House to infringe on the committee’s constitutionally protected right to conduct congressional oversight.
“It appears Donald Trump has something to hide,” Garcia said in a statement. “Let’s be clear: Congress’ authority comes from Article I of the Constitution, not from the permission of the White House.”
He added: “We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers.”
Garcia’s office said it had not received the letter as of Wednesday, and that he had become aware of it through news reports. The letter was first reported by Punchbowl News.
Josh Chafetz, a Georgetown University law professor who studies Congress’ constitutional powers, called the letter “completely laughable.”
“I have never seen anyone suggest that members of Congress could be held criminally liable for how they use their oversight power,” Chafetz said.
He noted that the three-page letter, with a dozen footnotes, does not specify which law Democrats may be violating.
“What crime?” Chafetz said. “What provision of federal law might they have violated? He doesn’t even gesture towards one.”
As Democrats prepare to retake control of Congress, they have vowed to investigate Trump and administration officials over alleged corrupt practices.
In an exchange with reporters Tuesday, Garcia said Democrats are already looking into Trump’s former chief of staff Susie Wiles and potential deals with political donors that may have resulted in exchanging money for policy changes.
“Just because you’re no longer in the administration, whether your name is Susie Wiles, whether it’s Kimberly Guilfoyle, whether it’s Corey Lewandowski, whether it’s Kristi Noem, you are being investigated and there needs to be accountability in that space,” Garcia said.
Hours after it was clear Democrats would win back control of the House in last week’s midterm elections, Garcia issued a two-word statement: “Lawyer up.”
Other Democrats were similarly blunt.
Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) said tech executives should brace for investigations, saying that there will be a need to “plant new forests for all of the subpoenas” Democrats will be printing. Rep. Analilia Mejia (D-N.J.) said Democrats would be handing out subpoenas “like Mardi Gras beads.”
Scharf pointed to such statements in his letter to argue there is concern about their oversight powers being abused.
“Abusive threats and public statements about the indiscriminate issuance of subpoenas, along with threats directed at prospective targets within the Administration make it abundantly clear that any forthcoming investigative processes will be deployed to harass and aggrandize, rather than to advance any legitimate legislative end,” he wrote.
The letter cited Supreme Court rulings holding that congressional investigations must serve a legislative purpose. Chafetz, however, said those cases don’t support Scharf’s argument.
Barabak: ‘An endless amount of corruption.’ In a Democratic House, Trump would face a reckoning
Rep. Robert Garcia is poised to lead the investigative Oversight Committee. The Long Beach Democrat has a robust agenda and long list of people to hold to account.
“Legislative purpose is incredibly broad. Almost anything has a legislative purpose,” he said. “Certainly, investigating wrongdoing in the executive branch is a core legislative purpose.”
And even if a court found an investigation lacked a legislative purpose, Chafetz said the target could refuse to comply with a subpoena but it would not mean the lawmakers committed a crime.
Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) said in an interview that the letter would not deter Democrats from conducting their investigations. But Padilla said the letter, like Trump’s appointment last week of Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff, is another sign that the president plans to double down on his agenda in the face of a Democratic Congress.
“And we’re going to double down as well,” Padilla said.
The White House approach “shouldn’t come as a surprise for anybody,” Padilla said. “The bullying tactics continue, the weaponization of the Department of Justice continues, but it just goes to show how scared the administration is of facing accountability.”
The White House did not respond to a request seeking comment on the letter.

How Nvidia CEO’s extramarital affair could cause collateral damage in Washington
Extramarital affairs are usually private matters. Jensen Huang’s has global implications. The 63-year-old is the leading face of the artificial intelligence revolution with his black leather jackets and fluff of grey hair. His leadership of Nvidia, which produces highly coveted computer chips, has given him a late-night-phone-call relationship with Trump, a promoter of the industry.
But Huang was also liaising with a Chinese businesswoman who has allegedly fed intelligence — as well as advanced chips — to China.
The woman, Alice Huang, is a former executive at the Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed. It’s a saga of personal betrayal, corporate espionage and high-tech development, and the fallout is spreading across Washington, with bipartisan calls for congressional investigations and the Department of Justice opening its own probe.
US futures climb and Nvidia shares stabilize in a brutal week for the chipmaker
U.S. futures are rising with crude still below $100 a barrel as shares of Nvidia stabilize in a brutal week for the chipmaker.
Nvidia was the single heaviest weight on the S&P 500 on Tuesday, but shares are up 3.7% in early trading Wednesday. They are still down almost 10% this week.
The company central to the artificial intelligence boom has been under pressure following revelations of CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a purported Chinese spy. The company’s board announced an investigation and Trump said the FBI is investigating the affair, which Huang has acknowledged and apologized for.
Joe Biden tells ‘People’ he wouldn’t have run again if he’d known he had cancer
Ahead of his memoir release, Biden told the magazine that he didn’t know he had cancer while he was president.
“If I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer,” he said, he “would’ve not gone forward, because I don’t think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running” for president.
Biden was diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer months after leaving office. He insisted he was able to perform his duties while he was president.
“I believe that on an objective basis, I was the best-equipped person to do the job,” he said.
Biden argued that age itself — he was 81 in his final year in office — was not disqualifying and meant he had experience and deep personal relationships with world leaders.
His White House memoir, “Promise Me, America,” will be released next Tuesday.
A note to ‘46’: Trump’s private message to Biden emerges in new White House memoir
Trump, who for years disputed his loss in the 2020 election and publicly decried the result as having been stolen from him by Democratic forces, privately lauded incoming President Joe Biden as someone he believed would “be true to yourself and the American people.”
That sentiment, along with others, was part of the letter Trump left for Biden upon leaving office in January 2021. Biden showed the note to some members of his staff after his inauguration in 2021 but didn’t let anyone read it, describing it later that day as “very generous” but otherwise saying he considered it to be private.
Inclusion of the letter in Biden’s “Promise Me, America,” his White House memoir slated for release Nov. 17, was first reported Tuesday by The New York Times. The Associated Press has reviewed a photocopy of the two-page letter, handwritten in Trump’s trademark black Sharpie on White House stationery and addressed “To ‘46,’” denoting Biden’s place as the 46th U.S. president.
Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio elected to lead House Republicans in the minority
Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio has won a party contest to serve as House Republican leader as the party prepares for its new role in the minority and a flurry of Democratic investigations aimed at its standard-bearer in the White House.
Jordan, chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, defeated Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana in a secret-ballot election of Republicans who will serve in the next Congress. Tuesday's vote was 106-73.
Jordan, 62, co-founded the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus. His candidacy appealed to those looking for new leadership in the wake of last week’s election debacle and to those who like his hard-hitting political style.
Jordan will inherit a historically small House Republican conference that is only beginning to grapple with its loss of power for Trump's final two years in office. Leading the party back to a House majority in 2028 is sure to be a stiff climb, given the scope of Democratic victories.

White House counsel Will Scharf issued the warning in a letter dated Monday to Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee.

In response, Scharf wrote in Monday’s letter that “threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

“Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate,” Garcia said. “The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse.”
Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. The Republican president and his White House have long denied any wrongdoing.
The Republican-led House Oversight Committee slammed the Trump administration on Tuesday for botching the public release of millions of pages …
Garcia also wants to look at the administration’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations. Other targets include Trump’s White House ballroom and other construction projects, as well as the Trump family’s role in mineral deals and Trump’s crypto dealings with special envoy Steve Witkoff.
Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a CNN interview that aired Sunday that “there could be” a crime to investigate if rhetoric from Democrats turned threatening. He appeared to strike a more conciliatory tone during an appearance in Missouri this week, saying “Congress has oversight authority. It always has, it always will. The Department of Justice, the federal government, works with Congress to address questions they have — whether it’s through subpoenas or letters — so we’re not going to stop working with Congress.”
“Nothing I’ve said this weekend, or in the past, should suggest otherwise,” he added.

WASHINGTON — The White House this week has issued an extremely unusual threat to the Democrat who will soon chair the House Oversight Committee.
In a Monday letter, White House counsel Will Scharf told Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) that his plans to request records and interviews from the administration next year could “cross the line into blatant criminality.”
Not only that, Scharf threatened Garcia that “issuing unlawful subpoenas with the intention of depriving citizens of their constitutional rights and privileges may warrant further investigation.”
It’s a shocking threat because conducting oversight of the executive branch, including through subpoenas, is one of the most basic functions of Congress. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that the power to conduct investigations is an inherent part of the legislative process. It’s hard to imagine any court allowing the Justice Department to prosecute a member of Congress for demanding information from the executive branch.
But Scharf claims in his letter, obtained by HuffPost and first reported by Punchbowl News, that Garcia’s public statements, including that members of the Trump administration should “lawyer up,” are malicious and improper because of other comments that allegedly envision administration officials going to jail. Scharf also makes the standard executive branch argument that Garcia’s eventual requests would lack a legitimate legislative purpose.
“Bizarrely, you have chalked your motives up to nothing more than ‘gay’ ‘pettiness’ rather than any legislative purpose and compared yourself to a demonic clown,” Scharf wrote, referring to Garcia’s comments on a podcast and a social media post with an image from the film “It.”
The letter is a signal that the Trump administration will be maximally hostile to the deluge of investigations it’s likely to face from the incoming Democratic Congress.
“It appears Donald Trump has something to hide,” Garcia said in a statement. “Let’s be clear: Congress’ authority comes from Article I of the Constitution, not from the permission of the White House. Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate.”
President Donald Trump on Saturday in a Truth Social post called Democrats’ threats to investigate the administration “illegal” and said he was “ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!”
The Trump administration has already attempted to criminally prosecute multiple Democratic members of Congress, including six lawmakers who participated in a video urging military servicemembers to disobey illegal orders. White House Threatens to Charge Democrats if They Investigate
The White House sent a chilling letter to Democrats warning that their investigations could be considered criminal behavior.
Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
The White House is threatening Democrats in Congress, warning them that investigating President Donald Trump could cross the line into criminal action.
Punchbowl News reports that White House counsel Will Scharf sent a letter on Monday to Democratic Representative Robert Garcia, the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, saying that congressional investigations “must further a legitimate executive task; Congress cannot employ them to exercise powers of criminal prosecution assigned to the Executive and the Judiciary.”
Garcia and his fellow Democrats have made “it abundantly clear that any forthcoming investigative processes will be deployed to harass and aggrandize, rather than to advance any legitimate legislative end,” Scharf claims, citing statements by incoming Democrats calling for the prosecution of ICE agents, trials for tech executives, and hearings for Cabinet secretaries like embattled Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
The letter is an extreme attempt to intimidate House Democrats into backing off Trump and his legally questionable actions, and it makes a mockery of the constitutional separation of powers, as well as checks and balances between the three branches of government. Scharf is taking a questionable Republican position that effectively says that Congress has no critical oversight over the executive branch.
The warning is rich, considering how the Trump administration has pushed sham prosecutions against members of Congress who told military and intelligence personnel not to follow illegal orders or who protested against ICE. That’s to say nothing of the targeting of many of Trump’s perceived enemies. It seems that the White House knows it has something to hide and thinks of itself as above the law.
Full List of Democrats Who Missed Hegseth Impeachment Vote—and Why
The Hegseth impeachment resolution failed after 11 Democrats didn’t show up to vote. Here’s where they say they were instead.
Representative Nancy Pelosi
Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images
Representative Nancy Pelosi
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has 11 Democratic House members to thank for tanking the nascent effort to impeach him.
House Republicans blocked Representative Thomas Massie’s articles of impeachment against Hegseth from reaching the floor by a 211–204 vote. While Republicans were initially concerned they lacked the party votes to block the resolution, it was 11 absent Democratic lawmakers who handed them a victory.
Their names are:
Melanie Stansbury (New Mexico)
Marilyn Strickland (Washington)
Julia Brownley (California)
Lou Correa (California)
Laura Gillen (New York)
Steven Horsford (Nevada)
Jonathan Jackson (Illinois)
Nancy Pelosi (California)
Brittany Pettersen (Colorado)
Haley Stevens (Michigan)
Frederica Wilson (Florida)
Some of those truant Democratic lawmakers said they were stuck in “bumper-to-bumper” traffic on their way back from a new member reception held by the Elect Democratic Women PAC, according to Axios’s Andrew Solender. That group’s offshoot, the EDW Action Fund, has served as a major pass-through for funds from United Democracy Project, a super PAC formed by the American Israeli Public Affairs Committee. It’s not clear which members were in attendance at the event.
Representative Katherine Clark, who as Democratic whip is responsible for organizing her party’s House members ahead of a vote, is also one of the founding members of EDW. Clark was not absent for the vote, and called the results a “disgrace.”
Of the 11 Democrats who missed the Hegseth vote, eight have received support from EDW or its action group, including Brownley, who sits on the organization’s executive board, and Stansbury, who serves on the board of directors.
House Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi, meanwhile, said she missed the vote because she flew back to San Francisco for the Swords to Plowshares 30th Annual Veterans Day Celebration. Horsford’s office said he had a personal emergency, and Correa previously said he was undergoing a medical procedure.
The resounding Democratic failure comes amid a tidal wave of calls for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries to step down following sweeping Democratic victories in the House and Senate. Jeffries faces criticism for failing to unite Democrats to mount a compelling challenge against the Trump administration. Now it appears that he couldn’t even get them to all show up for one important vote.
After the vote, Jeffries told Politico, “I haven’t had a conversation with anyone on the floor team about what may or may not have happened in terms of the Hegseth resolution, but this is not the end of it. It’s just the beginning.”
President Donald Trump called the results of Tuesday’s vote a total “exoneration” of Hegseth.
Van Hollen Calls Out Schumer for Siding With AIPAC and Crypto
Chris Van Hollen is speaking up as Democrats debate who can replace Chuck Schumer in the Senate.
Senators Chris Van Hollen and Chuck Schumer
Stephen Maturen/Getty Images
Senators Chris Van Hollen and Chuck Schumer
Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen is plotting out his position against Democratic leader Chuck Schumer.
“I am listening to all the people from around the country that were calling for big change,” Van Hollen said at the Popular Mandate national conference Tuesday, according to Semafor reporter David Weigel. “I am in the process right now of calling my colleagues.”
“We just saw democracy in America in action. We should bring a little more democracy to the United States Senate,” Van Hollen continued. “We have two newly-elected senators who would not be there if Schumer and the [Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee] had their way.”
Van Hollen then drew a line in the sand, arguing that Schumer and the DSCC had “sided with the crypto industry” and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, better known by the acronym AIPAC.
A wave of Democratic voices have been opposing Schumer’s leadership and establishment politics since the party won the majority in Congress in last week’s elections. Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen has emerged as a potential alternative, indicating a rising interest in progressive leadership. His office has received an “outpouring of calls and is now in active listening mode,” one source told Politico’s Playbook.
Van Hollen’s national profile rose last year when he traveled out of the country to visit his constituent Kilmar Ábrego García after García was illegally deported by the Trump administration to El Salvador’s notoriously lethal maximum security prison, CECOT.
Whether or not Van Hollen will officially commit himself against Schumer remains to be seen, though the Marylander has already started to draft an opposition platform that could put pressure on Schumer’s politics. On Tuesday, Van Hollen declared that the U.S. cannot spend “a penny more” on the Iran war, daring Donald Trump to either stop funding the war or face the possibility of a government shutdown.
So far, at least 10 major senators or senators-elect have either peeled away from Schumer outright or indicated interest in a different Senate majority leader. Another 14 have not yet committed as to whether they will support Schumer, according to an analysis published Monday by Primary Democrats. Altogether, that’s 24 Democrats—or nearly half of the at least 54 Democratic seats that will dominate the upper chamber come January.
But Schumer remains undeterred by the mounting opposition.
“I’m confident I will be elected majority leader,” Schumer said at a press conference Tuesday afternoon. “Our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war. We have great unity in our caucus and I’ll be proud to lead as majority leader.”
Disabled Woman Sues Trump Admin After ICE Dragged Her From Her Car
Aliya Rahman, a U.S. citizen, wants accountability after her violent arrest.
ICE agents detain Aliya Rahman after pulling her from a car on January 13 in Minneapolis.
Stephen Maturen/Getty Images
ICE agents detain Aliya Rahman after pulling her from a car on January 13 in Minneapolis.
A Minneapolis woman who was violently pulled out of her car and arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents while she was on her way to a doctor’s appointment in January is suing the federal government.
Aliya Rahman, a Minneapolis resident, filed the lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Minnesota Tuesday claiming that she was the victim of false arrest and imprisonment, negligent supervision, negligence, assault, and battery.
“I am one of many who have been impacted by this government’s vile abuse of power,” Rahman said in a statement. “And while this lawsuit stems from what happened in January, the terror did not start there and has not stopped.”
Rahman, who is autistic and has physical disabilities, was traveling to a medical appointment on January 13 during Operation Metro Surge, the federal government’s immigration crackdown in Minnesota’s twin cities. ICE agents surrounded her car and smashed her window after she said, “They needed to learn how to respect human beings,” her complaint states. They then dragged her out of the car and sent her to a federal detention facility for hours. She said that she was denied medical care while in ICE custody, and had to go to the hospital after losing consciousness.
Her violent arrest was captured on video and went viral online, and she later testified before Congress. She went on to attend President Trump’s State of the Union address in February as a guest of Representative Ilhan Omar, and was arrested by Capitol police for “disruption of Congress.”*
Rahman’s lawsuit comes after multiple attempts to hold ICE agents accountable. She filed a Federal Tort Claims Act claim alleging unlawful force and detention in April, and in June filed a federal complaint with the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Civil Rights and Civil Liberties. The tort claim was a prerequisite for Tuesday’s lawsuit.
Rahman’s attorney, Jessica Gingold of the MacArthur Justice Center, said at a news conference Tuesday that part of the lawsuit’s goal was identifying the agents responsible for the violent attack.
“We will find the names,” Gingold said. “We have their pictures…. We have a right to depose them. We have a right to get their records to understand who these individuals were who heard Aliya, frustrated and confused, and reacted with such violence.”
* This story has been updated to reflect Rahman’s arrest at the State of the Union.

sources.text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Democrats in the US House of Representatives, who will control key committees next year, are preparing investigations into what they say was President Donald Trump’s politicization and gutting of US spy agencies, including whether analysts have censored themselves to avoid retaliation. 
“There’s absolutely evidence that analysts are hesitant to write on topics that they think might be controversial. There’s absolutely evidence of a decline in morale in the analytic community because of the pressures that they are under,” US Representative Jim Himes, a Connecticut Democrat who will become chairman of the House intelligence committee in January, told Reuters on Tuesday.
There has been little scrutiny of the state of the US intelligence community by the Republican-run Congress during the first two years of Trump’s second term, during which the administration fired or forced out hundreds of officers and disrupted the production of analyses on key issues, including Iran.
Himes said that would change after he takes over the committee in January, when Democrats assume control of the House of Representatives and the Senate following their sweep of the November 3 midterm elections.
He did not disclose how the investigations would proceed, but said that one focus would be what he called retaliatory firings.
“We’re going to tell the story of the patriots who were fired because they said something that was inconsistent with what the president wanted to be true,” Himes said.
Former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard last year cut her agency’s staff by about 40%. CIA Director John Ratcliffe publicly pledged to reduce his workforce by more than 1,000 positions over several years. Both offered deferred-resignation programs that provided pay and benefits for employees who chose to leave.
The cuts included the firings of longtime intelligence analysts and officers from top posts, including at the National Intelligence Council, the analytical group overseen by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.
At least two of those fired were analysts involved in an assessment that contradicted the White House’s official policy on Venezuela.
The reductions have been viewed inside the intelligence agencies as a continuation of Trump’s campaign against what he called the “deep state,” a move critics say has drained the community of experience and expertise.
Reuters previously reported that some of Gabbard’s projects affiliated with her Director’s Initiative Group, a task force that revisited the 2020 election and the origins of COVID-19, created tensions inside the intelligence community.
That was particularly the case after Gabbard’s office revoked the security clearances of current and former intelligence officials a year ago. 
Gabbard’s actions caused a breakdown in intelligence sharing and cooperation inside the intelligence community and with Congress, as Reuters previously reported.
“The moment the intelligence community stops telling the truth to national leaders, you get into an Iraq war because of weapons of mass destruction that don’t exist,” Himes said.
Himes said he had reviewed a statutorily mandated intelligence community survey showing that, in 2025, the workforce had begun to “feel very real political pressure.”
He added he was working to declassify other internal intelligence community reporting that could potentially underscore the effects of the firings and politicization.
The committee, Himes said, will also probe the administration’s relationships with defense and intelligence contractors and US covert efforts overseas.

Scharf maintained that such rhetoric suggested Democrats intended to use their newly acquired subpoena powers for political purposes rather than legitimate oversight.
The letter accused Democrats of preparing investigations designed to “harass and aggrandize rather than to advance any legitimate legislative end.”
Garcia immediately rejected the warning, accusing the White House of attempting to intimidate Congress before Democrats even assume control of its investigative committees.
“It appears Donald Trump has something to hide,” Garcia said.
“Let’s be clear: Congress’ authority comes from Article I of the Constitution, not from the permission of the White House. Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate.”
Garcia insisted that the incoming Democratic majority would proceed with its planned investigations despite the administration’s warnings.
“We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers,” he declared.
Democrats have outlined an extensive investigative agenda targeting the Trump administration, including the president’s family business interests, cryptocurrency ventures, federal immigration enforcement, and the government’s handling of records connected to convicted offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Members of Congress additionally enjoy substantial protections under the Constitution’s Speech or Debate Clause, which generally shields legitimate legislative activities from executive branch interference.

“Abusive threats and public statements about the indiscriminate issuance of subpoenas, along with threats directed at prospective targets within the Administration make it abundantly clear that any forthcoming investigative processes will be deployed to harass and aggrandize rather than to advance any legitimate end,” he wrote.
Scharf accused Democrats of making “abusive and capricious threats” and said they are seeking to “abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with lawful functioning of government.”
Garcia said in response to Scharf that the White House is threatening to infringe on his committee’s right to conduct oversight.
“It appears Donald Trump has something to hide,” the California Democrat said in a statement. “Let’s be clear: Congress’ authority comes from Article I of the Constitution, not from the permission of the White House. Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate.”
Garcia accused the Trump administration of weaponizing the executive branch against Congress.
“We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers,” he said.
Following last week’s midterm elections, Democrats are poised to hold at least 254 seats in the House and 54 seats in the Senate, giving them control of congressional committees and subpoena power.
Garcia had a brief message to the Trump administration on the heels of Democrats’ rout of Republicans in the fight for control of Congress: “Lawyer up.”
Once he takes the gavel of the Oversight Committee, the panel is expected to look into the Trump family’s business dealings, corporate corruption, actions by federal immigration authorities and the scandal involving convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Garcia said his investigative agenda could also include:
- Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding festivities in the Bahamas that were partially paid for by a Russian oligarch.
- A $2 billion investment that the private equity fund of Mr. Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, received from Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund.
- The Trump family’s crypto ventures.
- Companies linked to the president’s sons that have received Pentagon contracts.
- Allegations of a pay-to-play scheme and other kickbacks related to Department of Homeland Security contracts.
- Corporate donations to fund the new White House ballroom.
Faced with investigations once Democrats regain congressional majorities, Mr. Trump on Sunday accused Democrats of threatening senior members of his administration and claimed they were engaging in “extortion.” The president said on Truth Social the Democrats “should be held accountable for this,” and he directed the Justice Department to look into their oversight push.
“These SLEAZEBAGS should go to jail for what they are doing,” he wrote in a second Truth Social post.
Democrats in Congress have in the past faced resistance from the White House in its efforts to investigate Mr. Trump and his administration. During the president’s first term, Democratic-led House committees sought a trove of Mr. Trump’s financial records from his accounting firm and two banks as part of an investigation into potential misconduct before and after he took office, whether he had undisclosed conflicts of interest and if he was complying with the Constitution.
Mr. Trump attempted to block the firms from complying with the subpoenas and took the dispute to the Supreme Court. In a 2020 decision, the high court declined to immediately give Congress access to the financial records, but reiterated that subpoenas must serve a “legitimate legislative purpose” and acknowledged that lawmakers have “significant legislative interests.”

sources.news_title: White House Warns Robert Garcia Over Trump Investigations
sources.text:
The White House has issued a warning to Rep. Robert Garcia, the California Democrat preparing to lead the House Oversight Committee, suggesting that certain investigations into Trump administration officials could expose lawmakers to criminal liability.
The warning, delivered in a November 9 letter from White House counsel Will Scharf, comes as Democrats prepare to take control of the House following the 2026 midterm elections. Garcia, who is expected to become chairman of the powerful oversight panel, has made clear that investigating the Trump administration will be a priority.
According to Punchbowl News, which first reported the letter, Scharf warned Garcia about the legal boundaries of congressional investigations. The White House argued that certain investigative actions could constitute criminal conduct, raising questions about how the administration intends to respond to Democratic oversight.

The letter represents an early confrontation between the Trump administration and the incoming Democratic House majority, particularly over Congress’s authority to investigate executive branch officials.
The House Oversight Committee is one of Congress’s principal investigative bodies. It has the authority to examine federal agencies, request government records, hold hearings and issue subpoenas compelling witnesses to testify or produce documents.
That authority is rooted in Congress’s constitutional responsibilities, including its power to oversee federal spending, examine government operations and consider legislation.
Garcia has rejected the White House’s warning and maintained that congressional investigations are a legitimate exercise of legislative authority.
The dispute centers on how far congressional investigators can go when examining the actions of executive branch officials. While Congress has broad investigative powers, those powers are not unlimited. Investigations must serve a legitimate legislative purpose, and lawmakers remain subject to applicable legal restrictions.
However, investigating government officials, requesting documents or questioning witnesses does not automatically constitute criminal conduct simply because the White House objects to the investigation.
The administration’s position could become particularly consequential if Garcia’s committee seeks testimony or records from senior Trump officials.
Congressional subpoenas can trigger legal disputes when the executive branch refuses to cooperate. Such conflicts may involve claims of executive privilege, a legal doctrine allowing the president and other executive officials to withhold certain confidential communications under specific circumstances.
Courts have historically played a role in resolving disputes between Congress and the executive branch, although those cases can take months or longer to resolve.
Attorney General Todd Blanche has also acknowledged Congress’s authority to conduct oversight, an important consideration as questions emerge about whether the Justice Department could become involved in future disputes.
The warning arrives before Garcia formally assumes the chairmanship, meaning the immediate confrontation concerns investigations that have not yet been conducted under his leadership.
For Democrats, control of the Oversight Committee would provide an institutional mechanism to investigate the Trump administration that they lacked while Republicans controlled the House.
As chairman, Garcia would be positioned to set the committee’s investigative agenda, schedule hearings and pursue subpoenas, subject to applicable House rules and legal requirements.
The White House, meanwhile, retains the ability to challenge congressional demands through legal proceedings and assert recognized protections over certain executive branch information.
The next major test will come when the new Congress convenes and the committee begins requesting documents or testimony from administration officials.
Whether the White House’s warning leads to criminal referrals, litigation or other formal action remains unclear. No criminal charge against Garcia has been established in connection with the warning.
The confrontation sets up a potential constitutional dispute over the balance of power between Congress and the White House, with the outcome likely to affect how aggressively lawmakers can investigate the administration during the remainder of Trump’s term.
